lead: The Saturday of the week of the Resurrection brings us back to the empty tomb, and then lifts our eyes upward. Mark tells of the women who came with spices on the first day of the week and found a young man in white where they expected a body. Colossians draws the conclusion for the baptized: if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, for your life is hidden with him. One reading tells what happened at the tomb; the other tells what it means for the way we live. The key words are raised, seek and hidden.

r.h: Seek the things that are above
set: These four verses are the hinge of the Letter to the Colossians. Chapters 1–2 have shown who Christ is and what Baptism has done: the believers were buried with him and raised with him (2:12). From 3:5 the letter turns to daily life: what to put to death, what to put on, how to live at home. The bridge between them is this short passage. Christian conduct grows out of what has already happened to us in Christ.
The teachers at Colossae urged rules about food and festivals and the worship of angels (2:16–23). The answer is not a new set of rules but a new direction: look to where Christ is.
str: v. 1: if raised with Christ, seek what is above, where Christ is seated.
v. 3: you have died; your life is hidden with Christ in God.
v. 4: when Christ appears, you will appear with him in glory.
kw: Not a place among the stars but the realm where Christ reigns with the Father. To seek it is to take one's measure from Christ rather than from what passes away.
The perfect tense: it has been hidden and remains so. Our true life is real now, but it is not yet visible. It is kept safe, as treasure is hidden to protect it.
The word for Christ's coming at the end. What is hidden now will be shown, and we will be shown with him.
vv: So if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.
“If” here means “since”. The writer does not doubt that they were raised; he builds on it. “Seated at the right hand” comes from Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse most often echoed in the New.
Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth,
This is not contempt for creation, which the same letter says was made in Christ and for him (1:16). “Things on earth” here means the list that follows in v. 5: what belongs to the old life.
for you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
When Christ who is your life is revealed, then you also will be revealed with him in glory.
Christ is not only the giver of our life; he is our life.
ch: The Catechism teaches that, united with Christ by Baptism, believers already truly share in the heavenly life of the risen Christ, but that this life remains hidden with Christ in God until he appears (CCC 1003, quoting this passage). The Church reads these verses at the feast of the Resurrection in many traditions. They are the Easter programme for the Christian life: we live on earth with our hearts where Christ is, and so we work on earth with hope.

r.h: He has been raised; he is not here
set: Mark has told us that some women watched the crucifixion from a distance (15:40–41) and saw where the body was laid (15:47). Now three of them return when the sabbath is over, with spices to anoint the body. They expect a corpse and a heavy stone. They find neither.

In the oldest Greek manuscripts the Gospel of Mark ends at v. 8. The verses that follow in our Bibles (16:9–20) were added early and are received by the Church as inspired and canonical Scripture. Some manuscripts also add a short ending after v. 8, which the NRSV prints in brackets.
str: vv. 1–2: the women come at sunrise on the first day of the week.
v. 3: their worry about the stone.
v. 4: the stone already rolled back.
vv. 5–7: the young man in white and his message.
kw: Mark does not call him an angel, but his white robe and his message show that he comes from God. Mark used the same word for the young man who ran away naked when Jesus was arrested (14:51–52). Many readers have noticed the contrast: one young man fled in shame, and this one sits robed in white.
A passive verb: God has raised him. The New Testament speaks both of Jesus rising and of the Father raising him (CCC 648–649).
In Greek the Gospel's last words are literally “they were afraid, for”. It is a startling ending. The fear is the holy fear of those who have met the work of God.
vv: They had been saying to one another, “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance to the tomb?”
They came anyway. Love set out before it knew how the obstacle would be removed.
Do not be alarmed; you are looking for Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has been raised; he is not here.
The risen one is the same Jesus of Nazareth who was crucified. The Resurrection does not erase the Cross; the crucified one is the one who lives.
But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going ahead of you to Galilee;
And Peter: the one who denied him three times is named. The message of Easter begins with mercy to the one who fell furthest.
So they went out and fled from the tomb, for terror and amazement had seized them; and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.
The silence cannot be the end, since we are reading the Gospel. The women's message did reach the disciples, and so it reached us.
ch: The Catechism notes that Mary Magdalene and the holy women were the first to encounter the Risen One, so that the women were the first messengers of the Resurrection, even to the apostles (CCC 641). St Thomas Aquinas, commenting on John, called Mary Magdalene the apostle of the apostles (in substance). The day of the women's visit, “the first day of the week”, became the Lord's Day, the day on which the Church gathers for the Holy Qurbana (CCC 2174).

qa: Why does Mark end with fear and silence?

Many scholars think Mark ended deliberately at v. 8, leaving the reader to answer the message the women first received in trembling: he is going ahead of you. Others think the original ending was lost. Either way the Church has received the longer ending (16:9–20) as part of Scripture, and Mark himself has already told us, through Jesus' own predictions, that the disciples will see him (14:28; 16:7).
Mark says the women came “when the sun had risen”. Do the Gospels disagree about the time?

The Gospels describe the same morning from different angles: “at early dawn” (Luke 24:1), “while it was still dark” (John 20:1), “very early … when the sun had risen” (Mark 16:2). The women set out in the dark and arrived as the day broke. The details differ; the testimony is one.
rite: In Syriac the first day of the week is called ḥad b-šabbā, “the first in the week”. Every Sunday is for us a little feast of the Resurrection. Our tradition loves the image of the East: the rising sun is a sign of the risen Lord, whose coming in glory will be like the lightning that “comes from the east” (Matthew 24:27). Tomorrow, New Sunday, closes the first week of the Resurrection with the confession of Mar Thoma. Today's epistle gives the attitude for that feast: hearts set where Christ is.
study: The women set out not knowing who would roll away the stone. What act of love am I putting off because I cannot see how the obstacle will be removed?
“And Peter”: whom do I need to name and include in the good news, even after a failure?
What would it mean, in the week ahead, to “seek the things that are above” in my work and family?
